questions.problem:
Consider the function $f,$ defined as 

$$
f(x)=[\begin{aligned}x-1 \\ {x}^{2} \\ {x}^{3}\end{aligned}].
$$

What is the shape of the total derivative of $f$ with respect to $x?$
questions.worked_solution:
The total derivative of a vector-valued function $f:R\to {R}^{m}$ with respect to a scalar $x$ is the column vector

$$
\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x}=[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂x} \\ \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂x} \\ ⋮ \\ \frac{∂{f}_{m}}{∂x}\end{aligned}]\in {R}^{m\times 1}.
$$

In our case, the function 

- acts on a scalar $x\in R,$ and

- outputs a vector $f(x)\in {R}^{3}.$

Therefore, the total derivative will be a column vector of shape $3\times 1.$

questions.problem:
Consider the function 

$$
f(x)=[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & 0 \\ 2 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot x,
$$

where the dot denotes matrix multiplication. What is the shape of the total derivative $\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x}?$
questions.worked_solution:
The total derivative of a vector-valued function $f:{R}^{n}\to {R}^{m}$ with respect to a vector $x\in {R}^{n}$ is the $m\times n$ matrix

$$
\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x}=[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂{x}_{n}} \\ \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂{x}_{n}} \\ ⋮ & ⋮ & ⋱ & ⋮ \\ \frac{∂{f}_{m}}{∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{∂{f}_{m}}{∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{∂{f}_{m}}{∂{x}_{n}}\end{aligned}]\in {R}^{m\times n}.
$$

In our case, the function multiplies a vector by a $3\times 3$ matrix. Thus, 

- it must act on $3$-dimensional column vectors as input, and

- output a $3$-dimensional column vector.

Therefore, $f:{R}^{3}\to {R}^{3},$ and the total derivative will be a $3\times 3$ matrix.

$$

questions.problem:
Consider the function $f:R\to {R}^{2},$ defined by 

$$
f(x)=[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡(x) \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡(x)\end{aligned}].
$$

What is the total derivative of $f$ with respect to $x$ at $x=\frac{\pi }{2}?$
questions.worked_solution:
The total derivative of a vector-valued function $f:R\to {R}^{m}$ with respect to a scalar $x$ is the column vector

$$
\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x}=[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂x} \\ \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂x} \\ ⋮ \\ \frac{∂{f}_{m}}{∂x}\end{aligned}]\in {R}^{m\times 1}.
$$

In our case, the function 

- acts on a scalar $x\in R,$ and

- outputs a vector $f(x)\in {R}^{2}$ defined by 

$$
f(x)=[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡(x) \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡(x)\end{aligned}].
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x} & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂x} \\ \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂x}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂}{∂x}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(x)) \\ \frac{∂}{∂x}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(x))\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(x) \\ -\operatorname{sin}⁡(x)\end{aligned}]\in {R}^{2\times 1}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate the total derivative at $x=\frac{\pi }{2}$ and get

$$
\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x}(\frac{\pi }{2})=[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2}) \\ -\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ -1\end{aligned}].
$$

questions.problem: Consider the function $f:{R}^{3}\to R$ defined by $f(x)={x}_{1}{x}_{2}+3{x}_{1}{x}_{3}+{x}_{2}{x}_{3}.$ What is the total derivative of $f$ with respect to $x$ at ${x}_{0}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0 \\ 2\end{aligned}]?$
questions.worked_solution:
The total derivative of a scalar-valued function $f:{R}^{n}\to R$ with respect to a vector $x\in {R}^{n}$ is the row vector

$$
\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x}=[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{∂f}{∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{∂f}{∂{x}_{n}}\end{aligned}]\in {R}^{1\times n}.
$$

In our case, the function 

- acts on a vector $x\in {R}^{3},$ and

- outputs a scalar $f(x)\in R$ defined by 

$$
f(x)={x}_{1}{x}_{2}+3{x}_{1}{x}_{3}+{x}_{2}{x}_{3}.
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x} & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{∂f}{∂{x}_{2}} & \frac{∂f}{∂{x}_{3}}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂}{∂{x}_{1}}({x}_{1}{x}_{2}+3{x}_{1}{x}_{3}+{x}_{2}{x}_{3}) & \frac{∂}{∂{x}_{2}}({x}_{1}{x}_{2}+3{x}_{1}{x}_{3}+{x}_{2}{x}_{3}) & \frac{∂}{∂{x}_{3}}({x}_{1}{x}_{2}+3{x}_{1}{x}_{3}+{x}_{2}{x}_{3})\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}{x}_{2}+3{x}_{3} & {x}_{1}+{x}_{3} & 3{x}_{1}+{x}_{2}\end{aligned}]\in {R}^{1\times 3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate the total derivative at ${x}_{0}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0 \\ 2\end{aligned}]$ and get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x}({x}_{0}) & =[\begin{aligned}0+3(2) & 1+2 & 3(1)+0\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}6 & 3 & 3\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
Consider the function $f:{R}^{2}\to R$ defined by

$$
f(x)={x}^{T}\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ 3 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot x,
$$

where the dot denotes matrix multiplication. What is the total derivative of $f$ with respect to $x?$
questions.worked_solution:
The total derivative of a scalar-valued function $f:{R}^{n}\to R$ with respect to a vector $x\in {R}^{n}$ is the row vector

$$
\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x}=[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{∂f}{∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{∂f}{∂{x}_{n}}\end{aligned}]\in {R}^{1\times n}.
$$

In our case, writing out the function $f(x)$ where $x=[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}],$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & =[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} & {x}_{2}\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ 3 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}+3{x}_{2} & {x}_{1}+{x}_{2}\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}] \\  & ={x}_{1}^{2}+3{x}_{1}{x}_{2}+{x}_{1}{x}_{2}+{x}_{2}^{2} \\  & ={x}_{1}^{2}+4{x}_{1}{x}_{2}+{x}_{2}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x} & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{∂f}{∂{x}_{2}}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂}{∂{x}_{1}}({x}_{1}^{2}+4{x}_{1}{x}_{2}+{x}_{2}^{2}) & \frac{∂}{∂{x}_{2}}({x}_{1}^{2}+4{x}_{1}{x}_{2}+{x}_{2}^{2})\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2{x}_{1}+4{x}_{2} & 4{x}_{1}+2{x}_{2}\end{aligned}]\in {R}^{1\times 2}.\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.problem:
Consider the function
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14217875/assets/4e1b8017187aa04115950f67cbae8c62e260002d8df6f8fb86339959b8738262.svg)
where the dot denotes matrix multiplication. What is the shape of the total derivative $\dfrac{\textrm{d} \mathbf{f}}{\textrm{d} \mathbf{x}}?$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
The total derivative of a vector-valued function $\mathbf{f}: \mathbb{R}^{n} \rightarrow \mathbb{R}^m$ with respect to a vector $\mathbf{x} \in \mathbb{R}^n$ is the $m \times n$ matrix
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14217875/assets/84a86b7e75b3c09396405d92062543f980f325b4871b591f8d6ad06d1f0fa4cc.svg)

In our case, the function multiplies a vector by a $2 \times 4$ matrix. Thus,

- it must act on $4$-dimensional column vectors as input, and

- output a $2$-dimensional column vector.

canonical_examples.name:
Example: 
                    Computing the Total Derivative of a Vector-Valued Function
canonical_examples.problem:
Consider the vector-valued function $\mathbf{f}: \mathbb{R}^{4} \rightarrow \mathbb{R}^2$ defined by
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14217875/assets/2e7f8144a8cb560911b65d4ca657148df69568184b1aca0e89b5551e0d3cdcae.svg)

What is $\dfrac{\textrm{d} \mathbf{f}}{\textrm{d} \mathbf{x}},$ the total derivative of $\mathbf{f}$ with respect to $\mathbf{x}$ at ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14217875/assets/adccb3fb0692529551c254d01387a1c1950ff044def046da83d1331fd9271ea1.svg)
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
The total derivative of a vector-valued function $\mathbf{f}: \mathbb{R}^{n} \rightarrow \mathbb{R}^m$ with respect to a vector $\mathbf{x} \in \mathbb{R}^n$ is the $m \times n$ matrix
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14217875/assets/01a79963b1871d82fdd7244b67eb2185cd9bc3e1f066d0def6366552677b32fe.svg)

In our case, writing out the function $\mathbf{f}(\mathbf{x})$ where ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14217875/assets/f621db9742637aa006cc2033c77d6d30cf664529fd94cc2db9964effa2c44ed5.svg), we get
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14217875/assets/4825869f62821be4a775d58c7e85c03948025be018489cabb460156f74d80a58.svg)

From here, we have $f_1(\mathbf{x}) = x_1 + 2x_2 + 4x_3 + 8x_4$ and $f_2(\mathbf{x}) = x_1 + 3x_2 + 9x_3 +27x_4.$ So, the total derivative is

$$
\begin{aligned}\,\,\,\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x} & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂{x}_{2}} & \frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂{x}_{3}} & \frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂{x}_{4}} \\ \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂{x}_{2}} & \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂{x}_{3}} & \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂{x}_{4}}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & 4 & 8 \\ 1 & 3 & 9 & 27\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Since the total derivative is a constant matrix, evaluating it at ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14217875/assets/5001c288fe848bed80ed10055323aad27c90d0acab2088baf9fc48ebe17b3f4a.svg) gives the same matrix.

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Computing the Total Derivative of a Vector-Valued Function

canonical_examples.name:
Example: 
                    Computing a 3-Tensor Derivative
canonical_examples.problem:
Consider a function $\mathbf{f}: \mathbb R^{2\times 3} \to \mathbb R^2$ defined by
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14217875/assets/7583605f8c8c3cd07389b8f31c6bfc4eaaf3a6488f226a05d5e0972e5272c2c8.svg)
Given that $a_{ij}$ denotes the entry of $\mathbf{A}$ in the intersection of the $i$th row and $j$th column, find the value of $\dfrac{\partial f_1}{\partial a_{12}}.$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
We can write the function $\mathbf{f}$ as
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14217875/assets/ed6fb0575a19c9afb201170a089841d0271e20e219c54c956e03f5d3e8c87f41.svg)

Thus,

$$
\dfrac{\partial f_1}{\partial a_{12}} = \dfrac{\partial}{\partial a_{12}} (-a_{11} + 3a_{12} + 7a_{13} ) = 3.
$$

tutorials.name: Introduction
tutorials.problem:
In this lesson, we’ll continue exploring the *total derivative* of a vector-valued function, which generalizes the derivative to functions with multiple inputs and outputs.

Suppose a transformation $\boldsymbol{f}:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^m$ is defined by 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14217875/assets/cd9132d6a0e934349ae58a0718e6320cba3dd8ae84de7df2e3fb98b391256b57.svg) 

where $f_1,f_2,\ldots,f_m$ are scalar functions with $n$ variables.

If $\boldsymbol f$ is differentiable at $\mathbf{x},$ then the **total derivative** of $\boldsymbol f$ at $\mathbf{x},$ denoted $\boldsymbol{f}'(\mathbf{x}),$ is given by the $m \times n$ matrix

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14217875/assets/c8fbc309a129b8e19db46aebff637e47259b629ef83c282a38b3b318c3a4f269.svg)

This is sometimes called the **Jacobian matrix** of $\boldsymbol{f}$ at $\mathbf{x}$. Each row corresponds to the derivative of one component function $f_i$, and each column corresponds to the rate of change of all the components of $\boldsymbol f$ with respect to one input variable $x_j$. This is sometimes called the **numerator layout** for derivatives because each row corresponds to each function component, which appears in the numerator positions of the partial derivatives.

Notice that if $f: \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}$ is a scalar-valued function, then the total derivative is a row vector given by
  ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14217875/assets/6ef756e82eb71d528a8f279863fd86efc8669658456a65879fba73d08e964bd5.svg)

On the other hand, if $\boldsymbol{f}: \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}^m$ is a vector-valued function of a single variable, then the total derivative is a column vector
  ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14217875/assets/cd232968d5ffff3040294f8093a42c91bccd3207f91bfc2f784cb53cad00441d.svg)

Now let’s get some practice by working through a few examples of total derivatives.

tutorials.title: Introduction
tutorials.content:
In this lesson, we’ll continue exploring the *total derivative* of a vector-valued function, which generalizes the derivative to functions with multiple inputs and outputs.

Suppose a transformation $\boldsymbol{f}:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^m$ is defined by 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14217875/assets/cd9132d6a0e934349ae58a0718e6320cba3dd8ae84de7df2e3fb98b391256b57.svg) 

where $f_1,f_2,\ldots,f_m$ are scalar functions with $n$ variables.

If $\boldsymbol f$ is differentiable at $\mathbf{x},$ then the **total derivative** of $\boldsymbol f$ at $\mathbf{x},$ denoted $\boldsymbol{f}'(\mathbf{x}),$ is given by the $m \times n$ matrix

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14217875/assets/c8fbc309a129b8e19db46aebff637e47259b629ef83c282a38b3b318c3a4f269.svg)

This is sometimes called the **Jacobian matrix** of $\boldsymbol{f}$ at $\mathbf{x}$. Each row corresponds to the derivative of one component function $f_i$, and each column corresponds to the rate of change of all the components of $\boldsymbol f$ with respect to one input variable $x_j$. This is sometimes called the **numerator layout** for derivatives because each row corresponds to each function component, which appears in the numerator positions of the partial derivatives.

Notice that if $f: \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}$ is a scalar-valued function, then the total derivative is a row vector given by
  ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14217875/assets/6ef756e82eb71d528a8f279863fd86efc8669658456a65879fba73d08e964bd5.svg)

On the other hand, if $\boldsymbol{f}: \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}^m$ is a vector-valued function of a single variable, then the total derivative is a column vector
  ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14217875/assets/cd232968d5ffff3040294f8093a42c91bccd3207f91bfc2f784cb53cad00441d.svg)

Now let’s get some practice by working through a few examples of total derivatives.

tutorials.name: Some Standard Derivatives
tutorials.problem:
Let’s examine examples of functions defined by a matrix of constants multiplied by a vector more carefully.

Consider the vector-valued function $\mathbf{f}: \mathbb{R}^{2} \rightarrow \mathbb{R}^3$ defined by
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14217875/assets/f81cbd9b797d1f1b05edd5f254d6735456e937355fe0e6692a4a830da925351b.svg) 

Suppose we want to compute the total derivative $\dfrac{\textrm{d} \mathbf{f}}{\textrm{d} \mathbf{x}}$ at the point ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14217875/assets/cd0b094634acde36ee93c2fb90c6f11ab56c2f675d27ba65077542d75cb451d6.svg).

The total derivative of a vector-valued function $\mathbf{f}: \mathbb{R}^{n} \rightarrow \mathbb{R}^m$ with respect to a vector $\mathbf{x} \in \mathbb{R}^n$ is the $m \times n$ matrix
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14217875/assets/6305cfe857f2228d471b85f859302a43046470f1d182b34abbf3ab4b362e7e07.svg)

In our case, writing out the function $\mathbf{f}(\mathbf{x})$ where ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14217875/assets/a8d36d7195af007d90a4f62cf213e28c7f51ced97168fb16d31a2c9192799b53.svg), we get
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14217875/assets/79110c30e4f827ccc401c0d8d9b8a08f35a88d12781d83c7e365171de0bbd67d.svg)

From here, we have 

$$
f_1(\mathbf{x}) = 3x_1 + 0 \cdot x_2, \qquad f_2(\mathbf{x}) = x_1 - x_2,\qquad f_3(\mathbf{x}) = 0 \cdot x_1 + 2x_2.
$$

 

So, the total derivative is

$$
\begin{aligned}\,\,\,\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x} & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂{x}_{2}} \\ \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂{x}_{2}} \\ \frac{∂{f}_{3}}{∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{∂{f}_{3}}{∂{x}_{2}}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}3 & 0 \\ 1 & -1 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Since this is independent of $\mathbf x,$ we also have

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14217875/assets/c187256b1ad2181f53482829d4d5076b0b09fc19f1d399aa41fb9da6ca0bc8f3.svg)

In general, if $\mathbf f:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^m$ is defined by

$$
\mathbf f(\mathbf x) = A\mathbf x
$$

where $A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}$ is constant and $\mathbf x\in\mathbb R^n,$ then

$$
\bbox[4pt,border: 1px solid lightgray]{\dfrac{\textrm d \mathbf f}{\textrm d \mathbf x} = A}.
$$

tutorials.title: Some Standard Derivatives
tutorials.content:
Let’s examine examples of functions defined by a matrix of constants multiplied by a vector more carefully.

Consider the vector-valued function $\mathbf{f}: \mathbb{R}^{2} \rightarrow \mathbb{R}^3$ defined by
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14217875/assets/f81cbd9b797d1f1b05edd5f254d6735456e937355fe0e6692a4a830da925351b.svg) 

Suppose we want to compute the total derivative $\dfrac{\textrm{d} \mathbf{f}}{\textrm{d} \mathbf{x}}$ at the point ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14217875/assets/cd0b094634acde36ee93c2fb90c6f11ab56c2f675d27ba65077542d75cb451d6.svg).

The total derivative of a vector-valued function $\mathbf{f}: \mathbb{R}^{n} \rightarrow \mathbb{R}^m$ with respect to a vector $\mathbf{x} \in \mathbb{R}^n$ is the $m \times n$ matrix
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14217875/assets/6305cfe857f2228d471b85f859302a43046470f1d182b34abbf3ab4b362e7e07.svg)

In our case, writing out the function $\mathbf{f}(\mathbf{x})$ where ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14217875/assets/a8d36d7195af007d90a4f62cf213e28c7f51ced97168fb16d31a2c9192799b53.svg), we get
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14217875/assets/79110c30e4f827ccc401c0d8d9b8a08f35a88d12781d83c7e365171de0bbd67d.svg)

From here, we have 

$$
f_1(\mathbf{x}) = 3x_1 + 0 \cdot x_2, \qquad f_2(\mathbf{x}) = x_1 - x_2,\qquad f_3(\mathbf{x}) = 0 \cdot x_1 + 2x_2.
$$

 

So, the total derivative is

$$
\begin{aligned}\,\,\,\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x} & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂{x}_{2}} \\ \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂{x}_{2}} \\ \frac{∂{f}_{3}}{∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{∂{f}_{3}}{∂{x}_{2}}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}3 & 0 \\ 1 & -1 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Since this is independent of $\mathbf x,$ we also have

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14217875/assets/c187256b1ad2181f53482829d4d5076b0b09fc19f1d399aa41fb9da6ca0bc8f3.svg)

In general, if $\mathbf f:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^m$ is defined by

$$
\mathbf f(\mathbf x) = A\mathbf x
$$

where $A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}$ is constant and $\mathbf x\in\mathbb R^n,$ then

$$
\bbox[4pt,border: 1px solid lightgray]{\dfrac{\textrm d \mathbf f}{\textrm d \mathbf x} = A}.
$$

tutorials.name: Tensor Derivatives
tutorials.problem:
We've learned that the derivative of a vector-valued function is a Jacobian matrix. Now imagine the input to our function $\mathbf f$ is a matrix instead of a vector. In such cases, the Jacobian matrix must expand to account for two input dimensions.

Suppose we have a transformation $\boldsymbol{f} : \mathbb{R}^{m \times n} \to \mathbb{R}^p$ that maps a matrix $\mathbf{A} \in \mathbb{R}^{m \times n}$ to a vector $\mathbf{f}(\mathbf{A}) \in \mathbb{R}^p$, defined as

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14217875/assets/f7b9ca5880f164c28b490fd4a215a56769e426bdde8111a24e6530c03d83b937.svg)

where each $f_i$ is a scalar-valued function of all the entries of the matrix $\mathbf{A}.$

Since the input $\mathbf{A}$ varies along two dimensions (rows and columns), and the output $\mathbf{f}(\mathbf{A})$ varies along one (a vector with $p$ components), the total derivative of $\mathbf f,$ which we denote as 

$$
\dfrac{\textrm{d}\mathbf{f}}{\textrm{d}\mathbf{A}}
$$

is naturally represented as a *three-dimensional object!* The technical name for this object is a **tensor**. Since it is a three-dimensional object, this particular tensor is a **third-order tensor** (or $3$-**tensor**).

To capture a meaningful derivative, we must differentiate each component $f_i$ with respect to *every element of the matrix* $\mathbf A.$ We can visualize this as a stack of matrices, or layers, as shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14217875/assets/d533d4d2e387c8c9f177b9dafe939b58c1f1d7db2f03e9df2059fa9f7cbe22c5.png)

Let's apply this concept to a specific example in the next slide.

tutorials.title: Tensor Derivatives
tutorials.content:
We've learned that the derivative of a vector-valued function is a Jacobian matrix. Now imagine the input to our function $\mathbf f$ is a matrix instead of a vector. In such cases, the Jacobian matrix must expand to account for two input dimensions.

Suppose we have a transformation $\boldsymbol{f} : \mathbb{R}^{m \times n} \to \mathbb{R}^p$ that maps a matrix $\mathbf{A} \in \mathbb{R}^{m \times n}$ to a vector $\mathbf{f}(\mathbf{A}) \in \mathbb{R}^p$, defined as

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14217875/assets/f7b9ca5880f164c28b490fd4a215a56769e426bdde8111a24e6530c03d83b937.svg)

where each $f_i$ is a scalar-valued function of all the entries of the matrix $\mathbf{A}.$

Since the input $\mathbf{A}$ varies along two dimensions (rows and columns), and the output $\mathbf{f}(\mathbf{A})$ varies along one (a vector with $p$ components), the total derivative of $\mathbf f,$ which we denote as 

$$
\dfrac{\textrm{d}\mathbf{f}}{\textrm{d}\mathbf{A}}
$$

is naturally represented as a *three-dimensional object!* The technical name for this object is a **tensor**. Since it is a three-dimensional object, this particular tensor is a **third-order tensor** (or $3$-**tensor**).

To capture a meaningful derivative, we must differentiate each component $f_i$ with respect to *every element of the matrix* $\mathbf A.$ We can visualize this as a stack of matrices, or layers, as shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14217875/assets/d533d4d2e387c8c9f177b9dafe939b58c1f1d7db2f03e9df2059fa9f7cbe22c5.png)

Let's apply this concept to a specific example in the next slide.

tutorials.name: A Worked Example
tutorials.problem:
Suppose we have the function $\mathbf f: \mathbb R^{3\times2} \to \mathbb R^{2},$ defined as

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14217875/assets/8d7f629f4b82087a1d23ef1253ce7eb98ca760310d92a2ac8cf8c3fd3a4d9473.svg)

We calculate the derivatives of $\mathbf f$ layer by layer as follows:

- **Layer 1**: The derivatives of the first component $f_1$ with respect to $\mathbf A.$
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14217875/assets/c4dab9446396e82d20ebbb38e3aabce9908565aeb7aeb48f2804a271d6ddf66f.svg)

- **Layer 2**: The derivatives of the second component $f_2$ with respect to $\mathbf A.$
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14217875/assets/ce7e31c8c3faf75aa7980a0e4f5f707f84f116e97b30c8b0dbd504bcfb4822c8.svg)

Combining these layers into a 3D block, we get the total derivative (a $3$-tensor in $\mathbb R^{2\times3\times2}$):

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14217875/assets/3d6eeebb92218d4f0995dbccd74b444da112f0e55b22ade0bbaa0259e06e9bb0.png)

You've probably realized by now that working with 3-tensors directly is cumbersome! So, rather than trying to visualize the full tensor all at once, focusing on its components is often helpful. Generally,

$$
\left( \dfrac{\textrm{d}\mathbf{f}}{\textrm{d}\mathbf{A}} \right)_{i, j, k} = \dfrac{\partial f_i}{\partial a_{jk}}
$$

is a *scalar* representing the derivative of the $i$th output component with respect to the element $a_{jk}$ of the matrix $\mathbf A.$

For example, the derivative of $f_{\color{red}1}$ with respect to $a_{{\color{blue}3},{\color{blue}2}}$ corresponds to the component at index $({\color{red}1},{\color{blue}3},{\color{blue}2})$ of a tensor. In our example, we saw that
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14217875/assets/4fa3d21f5d62bd01491c49b3351cdd3cf751a7ad793509d1c2b3846e4f6825cd.svg)

Looking at the ${\color{red}1}$st layer (front face), row ${\color{blue}3},$ column ${\color{blue}2},$ we have

$$
\left(\dfrac{\textrm d \mathbf f}{\textrm d \mathbf A}\right)_{{\color{red}1}, {\color{blue}3}, {\color{blue}2}} = \bbox[4pt,border: 1px solid lightgray]{0}.
$$

Derivatives of matrix functions arise in optimization problems, machine learning (e.g., backpropagation through layers), and physics (e.g., tensor fields). Understanding their structure is key to efficient computation and interpretation.

tutorials.title: A Worked Example
tutorials.content:
Suppose we have the function $\mathbf f: \mathbb R^{3\times2} \to \mathbb R^{2},$ defined as

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14217875/assets/8d7f629f4b82087a1d23ef1253ce7eb98ca760310d92a2ac8cf8c3fd3a4d9473.svg)

We calculate the derivatives of $\mathbf f$ layer by layer as follows:

- **Layer 1**: The derivatives of the first component $f_1$ with respect to $\mathbf A.$
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14217875/assets/c4dab9446396e82d20ebbb38e3aabce9908565aeb7aeb48f2804a271d6ddf66f.svg)

- **Layer 2**: The derivatives of the second component $f_2$ with respect to $\mathbf A.$
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14217875/assets/ce7e31c8c3faf75aa7980a0e4f5f707f84f116e97b30c8b0dbd504bcfb4822c8.svg)

Combining these layers into a 3D block, we get the total derivative (a $3$-tensor in $\mathbb R^{2\times3\times2}$):

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14217875/assets/3d6eeebb92218d4f0995dbccd74b444da112f0e55b22ade0bbaa0259e06e9bb0.png)

You've probably realized by now that working with 3-tensors directly is cumbersome! So, rather than trying to visualize the full tensor all at once, focusing on its components is often helpful. Generally,

$$
\left( \dfrac{\textrm{d}\mathbf{f}}{\textrm{d}\mathbf{A}} \right)_{i, j, k} = \dfrac{\partial f_i}{\partial a_{jk}}
$$

is a *scalar* representing the derivative of the $i$th output component with respect to the element $a_{jk}$ of the matrix $\mathbf A.$

For example, the derivative of $f_{\color{red}1}$ with respect to $a_{{\color{blue}3},{\color{blue}2}}$ corresponds to the component at index $({\color{red}1},{\color{blue}3},{\color{blue}2})$ of a tensor. In our example, we saw that
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14217875/assets/4fa3d21f5d62bd01491c49b3351cdd3cf751a7ad793509d1c2b3846e4f6825cd.svg)

Looking at the ${\color{red}1}$st layer (front face), row ${\color{blue}3},$ column ${\color{blue}2},$ we have

$$
\left(\dfrac{\textrm d \mathbf f}{\textrm d \mathbf A}\right)_{{\color{red}1}, {\color{blue}3}, {\color{blue}2}} = \bbox[4pt,border: 1px solid lightgray]{0}.
$$

Derivatives of matrix functions arise in optimization problems, machine learning (e.g., backpropagation through layers), and physics (e.g., tensor fields). Understanding their structure is key to efficient computation and interpretation.
